teach:
Week 3 Science: Cells — Cell Theory, Organelles, Photosynthesis, Cellular Respiration, and Energy

Objectives

  • State the three parts of the cell theory and use them to judge statements about living things.
  • Name the main organelles and their jobs, and tell plant, animal, and bacterial cells apart.
  • Write and explain the equations for photosynthesis and cellular respiration, including where each happens and how the two are connected.
  • Trace the flow of energy from sunlight to glucose to ATP.
  • Answer GED-style questions based on cell diagrams and on experiments about photosynthesis and respiration.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in two colors (one for reactants, one for products).
  • Printed or on-screen copy of this week's Student Lesson and Study Notes.
  • Blank paper for each student to sketch a plant cell and an animal cell side by side.
  • This week's 12 practice items (course page) for independent practice.

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5"Living or not, and how do you know?" plus one recall question on variables from Week 1.
Direct instruction20Cell theory; cell types; organelles; plant vs. animal cells; photosynthesis and respiration equations; energy flow; Worked Examples 1–3.
Guided practice15The floating leaf disk experiment: students identify variables, the process, and the conclusion with teacher support.
Independent practice15Practice items 1–12 on the course page (finish for homework if needed).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; preview the exit ticket, study plan, and this week's Practice GED.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Write on the board: a mushroom, a rock, a drop of pond water with bacteria in it, a wooden table, a blade of grass. Ask: "Which of these is made of living cells right now? How could a scientist check?"

Then ask one review question: "In an experiment testing whether light color affects plant growth, what is the independent variable?"

Answers: The mushroom, the bacteria in the pond water, and the grass are made of living cells. The rock was never made of cells. The table was made from cells (wood) but those cells are dead now. A scientist could check with a microscope. The review answer: light color is the independent variable (it is what the experimenter changes).

Bridge: "Everything on the 'living' list is made of cells. Today we learn what cells are, what is inside them, and how they get and use energy."

Direct Instruction (20 minutes) — Talking Points

1. The cell theory. Robert Hooke named "cells" in 1665 after viewing cork under a microscope. By the mid-1800s, scientists including Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow had built the cell theory. Teach it as three statements:

  1. All living things are made of one or more cells.
  2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
  3. All cells come from cells that already exist (by cell division).

Point out what the theory does not say: it does not say all cells have a nucleus, and it does not say all cells look alike.

2. Two big kinds of cells. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) are small and simple. They have DNA, ribosomes, cytoplasm, and a cell membrane, but no nucleus and no membrane-covered organelles. Eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi, protists) have a nucleus that holds their DNA and many membrane-covered organelles. Memory hook: "Pro = no nucleus; Eu = do have one."

3. Organelles: a cell is like a factory. Use the factory comparison to make the jobs stick.

OrganelleJobFactory comparison
Cell membraneThin, flexible boundary; controls what enters and leavesSecurity gate
NucleusHolds DNA; controls the cell's activitiesMain office with the blueprints
CytoplasmGel-like fluid that fills the cell and holds the organellesFactory floor
RibosomesBuild proteinsAssembly workers
ER and Golgi apparatusMake, package, and ship proteins and fatsConveyor belts and shipping
MitochondriaCellular respiration: release energy from glucose as ATPPower plant
VacuoleStores water, food, and wastesStorage tank
Chloroplasts (plants and algae)Photosynthesis: capture light energy and make glucoseSolar panels
Cell wall (plants, fungi, most bacteria)Stiff outer layer outside the membrane; support and protectionOuter brick wall

4. Plant vs. animal cells. Have students sketch both as you describe them. A plant cell is boxy, with a stiff cell wall outside the membrane, green chloroplasts, a large central vacuole that can fill most of the cell, and the nucleus pushed toward one side. An animal cell is rounder or irregular, has only a cell membrane on the outside, no chloroplasts, and small vacuoles if any. Both have a nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, ER, Golgi, and mitochondria.

Say it twice: plants have mitochondria too. Plants make glucose by photosynthesis, but they still have to break that glucose down by cellular respiration to get usable energy.

5. Photosynthesis. Write the equation and color-code it: reactants (inputs) in one color, products (outputs) in the other.

Photosynthesis (in chloroplasts):
6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2

In words: carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen

Talking points: carbon dioxide enters through tiny pores in leaves; water comes up from the roots; the green pigment chlorophyll captures light. Light energy is stored as chemical energy in glucose. Oxygen is released as a waste product; it is the oxygen we breathe.

6. Cellular respiration.

Cellular respiration (in mitochondria):
C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP)

In words: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

Talking points: cells break down glucose and store the released energy in ATP, the cell's "energy currency," which powers movement, growth, and repair. Some energy is always lost as heat, which is why your body is warm. Respiration happens in plants and animals, day and night.

Without oxygen: some cells can use fermentation (anaerobic respiration). Yeast make carbon dioxide and alcohol (the bubbles in rising bread dough). Hard-working human muscles can make lactic acid. Fermentation releases only 2 ATP per glucose; aerobic respiration releases roughly 30 or more.

7. The two processes are mirror images. The products of photosynthesis (glucose and oxygen) are the reactants of respiration, and the products of respiration (carbon dioxide and water) are the reactants of photosynthesis. Energy enters living things as sunlight, is stored in glucose, and is released as ATP and heat. Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

Sunlight → (photosynthesis) → chemical energy in glucose → (respiration) → ATP → work in the cell + heat

Worked Example 1 — Identify the cell type

Problem: A lab describes three cells. Cell X has a cell wall, ribosomes, and a loop of DNA floating in the cytoplasm, but no nucleus. Cell Y has a cell wall, a nucleus, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole. Cell Z has a nucleus and mitochondria but no cell wall and no chloroplasts. Classify each.

Solution:

  • Cell X: no nucleus means prokaryotic, so it is a bacterium. (The cell wall does not make it a plant; most bacteria have walls.)
  • Cell Y: nucleus means eukaryotic; cell wall + chloroplasts + large central vacuole means a plant cell.
  • Cell Z: nucleus means eukaryotic; no wall and no chloroplasts means an animal cell.

Teaching point: Check the nucleus first (prokaryote or eukaryote), then look for wall and chloroplasts.

Worked Example 2 — Read the photosynthesis equation

Problem: Use 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2. (a) Name the reactants and products. (b) Show that the number of each kind of atom is the same on both sides. (c) How many molecules of oxygen are released for each molecule of glucose made?

Solution:

(a) Reactants: carbon dioxide and water (light supplies energy, not atoms). Products: glucose and oxygen.

(b) Left side: 6CO2 has 6 C and 6 × 2 = 12 O. 6H2O has 6 × 2 = 12 H and 6 O. Total: 6 C, 12 H, 12 + 6 = 18 O.
Right side: C6H12O6 has 6 C, 12 H, 6 O. 6O2 has 6 × 2 = 12 O. Total: 6 C, 12 H, 6 + 12 = 18 O.
Both sides: 6 C, 12 H, 18 O. Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.

(c) The coefficient of O2 is 6 and glucose has a coefficient of 1, so 6 molecules of oxygen per glucose.

Worked Example 3 — Interpret an indicator experiment

Problem: Bromothymol blue (BTB) is a dye that is blue when there is little carbon dioxide in water and turns yellow as carbon dioxide increases. A student fills four sealed tubes with the same green-tinted BTB water and places them in bright light for 24 hours.

TubeContentsColor after 24 hours in light
1Water snailYellow
2Water plantBlue
3Snail + plantGreen (no change)
4BTB water onlyGreen (no change)

Explain each result. Then predict Tube 2's color if it were kept in the dark for 24 hours.

Solution:

  • Tube 1: the snail carries out cellular respiration and releases CO2, so the BTB turns yellow.
  • Tube 2: in light, the plant's photosynthesis uses CO2 faster than its respiration makes it, so CO2 drops and the BTB turns blue.
  • Tube 3: the plant uses about as much CO2 as the snail adds, so the color stays about the same.
  • Tube 4: the control. It shows the BTB does not change color on its own in light.
  • Prediction: in the dark, the plant cannot photosynthesize but still respires, so CO2 builds up and the BTB turns yellow.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Read aloud. Students answer on paper; call on volunteers, then reveal.

Scenario: A student cuts 30 small, equal-sized disks from spinach leaves. She soaks them in a baking soda solution (which supplies carbon dioxide) and removes the air from inside them, so all of the disks sink. She puts 10 disks into each of three identical cups of the same solution at the same temperature. Cup A sits 10 cm from a lamp, Cup B sits 50 cm from the same lamp, and Cup C is covered with a box so it is dark. As the disks photosynthesize, gas builds up inside them and they float. She records how long it takes for 5 of the 10 disks to float.

CupLightTime for 5 disks to float
ABright (10 cm)8 minutes
BDim (50 cm)17 minutes
CDarkNo disks floated after 30 minutes
  1. What is the independent variable?
  2. What is the dependent variable?
  3. What gas makes the disks float, and which process produces it?
  4. What is the purpose of Cup C?
  5. Why did the student use baking soda solution?
  6. Write one conclusion the data support.

Answers:

  1. The amount of light (light intensity, set by distance from the lamp).
  2. The time it takes for 5 of the 10 disks to float.
  3. Oxygen, produced by photosynthesis.
  4. Cup C is the control. With no light, there is no photosynthesis, so it shows the disks do not float for some other reason.
  5. Photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide. The baking soda makes sure the disks have plenty, so carbon dioxide does not limit the results.
  6. Sample: Disks in brighter light floated faster, so the rate of photosynthesis increased as light intensity increased. Light is needed for the disks to float.

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students complete practice items 1–12 on the course page while you circulate. Unfinished items become homework.

Checks for Understanding (use during the wrap-up)

  • "What are the three parts of the cell theory?" Expected: all living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; all cells come from existing cells.
  • "Name three parts a plant cell has that an animal cell does not." Expected: cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole.
  • "Where does photosynthesis happen? Cellular respiration?" Expected: chloroplasts; mitochondria.
  • "What goes into photosynthesis? What comes out?" Expected: carbon dioxide, water, and light energy go in; glucose and oxygen come out.
  • "Do plants carry out cellular respiration?" Expected: yes, all the time, in their mitochondria.
  • "What is ATP?" Expected: the molecule cells use to carry and spend energy.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

"Plants do photosynthesis; animals do respiration." Correction: plants do both. Ask, "How does a plant's root cell, deep underground with no light, get energy?" (By respiring glucose made in the leaves.)

Reversing the equations. Students put oxygen in as an input to photosynthesis. Correction: plants release the oxygen we breathe, so oxygen is a product of photosynthesis. Animals breathe out carbon dioxide, so CO2 is a product of respiration.

"Mitochondria make energy." Correction: energy cannot be created. Mitochondria release energy stored in glucose and store it in ATP.

Mixing up cell wall and cell membrane. Correction: every cell has a membrane. The wall is an extra stiff layer outside the membrane in plants, fungi, and most bacteria.

Differentiation

Support: Give a partly labeled plant cell and animal cell sketch and have students fill in the missing names. Provide the factory comparison table as a reference card. Teach the equations in words first ("carbon dioxide plus water makes sugar plus oxygen") before adding chemical formulas. Use the phrase "Photosynthesis puts energy in the sugar; respiration takes energy out."

Stretch: Ask students to explain, using both equations, why the amount of carbon dioxide in the air near a forest is lower during the day than at night. (During the day, photosynthesis removes CO2 faster than respiration adds it; at night only respiration happens.)

How This Shows Up on the GED

Life science is about 40% of the GED Science test, and cell structure and energy are core topics. Expect a diagram described or shown with labeled parts, an equation, or a short experiment with a data table or graph. Typical wording:

  • "Which labeled structure is the site of photosynthesis?"
  • "Which structure would be found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell?"
  • "Based on the equation, which substances are the reactants of cellular respiration?"
  • "Which statement best explains why muscle cells contain many mitochondria?"
  • "Which conclusion is best supported by the data?"

Formats include multiple choice, drop-down menus that complete a sentence about a process, drag-and-drop sorting (for example, plant-only vs. both), fill-in-the-blank calculations (a mean or rate from trials), and hot spots (clicking a structure on a diagram or a sentence in a lab report). Teach students to read every equation as "inputs → outputs" before answering.

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Run the checks for understanding above, then preview the exit ticket, study plan, and this week's Practice GED.
student:
Cells: The Building Blocks of Life and How They Use Energy

Every living thing, from bacteria to oak trees to you, is made of cells. On the GED Science test you will see cell diagrams, equations, and experiments about how cells get energy. This lesson gives you the key facts and a method for each kind of question.

1. The cell theory

Scientists first saw cells through microscopes in the 1600s. Over the next two hundred years, they agreed on three main ideas, called the cell theory:

  1. All living things are made of one or more cells.
  2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
  3. All cells come from cells that already exist.

Notice what is not in the list: the cell theory does not say every cell has a nucleus.

2. Two kinds of cells

  • Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) are small and simple. They have DNA, ribosomes, cytoplasm, and a cell membrane, but no nucleus.
  • Eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi) have a nucleus and many organelles wrapped in membranes.

Memory hook: "Pro = no nucleus. Eu = do."

3. Organelles and their jobs

An organelle is a small structure inside a cell that does a specific job. Think of a cell as a factory.

OrganelleJobThink of it as
Cell membraneControls what enters and leavesSecurity gate
NucleusHolds DNA; controls the cellMain office
CytoplasmFluid that holds the organellesFactory floor
RibosomesMake proteinsAssembly workers
MitochondriaRelease energy from glucose (cellular respiration)Power plant
ChloroplastsCapture light and make glucose (photosynthesis)Solar panels
VacuoleStores water, food, and wastesStorage tank
Cell wallStiff outer layer for supportBrick wall

4. Plant cells vs. animal cells

Picture a plant cell as a box: a stiff cell wall on the outside, a cell membrane just inside it, a huge water-filled vacuole in the middle, green chloroplasts scattered around the edges, and the nucleus pushed to one side. Picture an animal cell as a soft, roundish bag: a cell membrane on the outside, the nucleus near the center, and no cell wall or chloroplasts.

PartPlant cellAnimal cell
Cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, ribosomesYesYes
MitochondriaYesYes
Cell wallYesNo
ChloroplastsYes (in green parts)No
VacuoleOne large central vacuoleSmall, if any
ShapeBoxy, fixedRound or irregular

Common mistake: thinking plants have no mitochondria. Plants make their own food, but they still need mitochondria to release the energy from that food.

5. Photosynthesis: storing the sun's energy

Plants and algae use light energy to make glucose (a sugar) in their chloroplasts.

6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2

carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen

The substances on the left are the reactants (what goes in). The substances on the right are the products (what comes out). Carbon dioxide comes from the air, water comes from the roots, and the green pigment chlorophyll captures the light. The light energy ends up stored as chemical energy in glucose. Oxygen is released into the air.

6. Cellular respiration: releasing the energy

All living cells, in plants and animals, break down glucose to get usable energy. This happens in the mitochondria.

C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP)

glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

The energy is stored in a molecule called ATP, which the cell "spends" to move, grow, and repair itself. Some energy is always lost as heat. When oxygen is scarce, some cells use fermentation, which releases much less energy (yeast make carbon dioxide and alcohol; tired muscles make lactic acid).

The mirror trick: respiration is photosynthesis run backward. The products of one are the reactants of the other. If you remember one equation, flip it to get the other. Energy flows in one direction: sunlight → glucose → ATP → work and heat.

Worked Examples

Example 1. A cell has a nucleus, mitochondria, and a cell membrane, but no cell wall and no chloroplasts. What kind of cell is it?

Step 1: It has a nucleus, so it is eukaryotic (not a bacterium).
Step 2: No cell wall and no chloroplasts, so it is not a plant cell.
Answer: an animal cell.

Example 2. Which substances are used up during cellular respiration?

Step 1: Find the equation: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy.
Step 2: "Used up" means reactants, the left side of the arrow.
Answer: glucose and oxygen.

Example 3. A student puts a water plant in a test tube under a lamp and counts the oxygen bubbles it gives off. In three 1-minute trials, she counts 18, 21, and 24 bubbles. She moves the lamp farther away and counts 9, 11, and 10. What do the results show?

Step 1: Find each mean. Close: (18 + 21 + 24) ÷ 3 = 63 ÷ 3 = 21 bubbles per minute. Far: (9 + 11 + 10) ÷ 3 = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 bubbles per minute.
Step 2: Connect to the process. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, so more bubbles means more photosynthesis.
Answer: With less light, the plant photosynthesized more slowly (about 10 instead of 21 bubbles per minute).

Try It

1. Which part of the cell theory explains why a cut on your skin can heal by growing new skin cells?

Show answer

"All cells come from cells that already exist." New skin cells are made when existing skin cells divide.

2. A cell has a cell wall, ribosomes, and DNA, but no nucleus. Is it a plant cell, an animal cell, or a bacterium?

Show answer

A bacterium. No nucleus means prokaryotic. Plant cells have a nucleus.

3. Name the two products of photosynthesis.

Show answer

Glucose and oxygen.

4. A potted plant is kept in a dark closet for two days. Which process does it continue to carry out: photosynthesis, cellular respiration, or both?

Show answer

Cellular respiration only. Photosynthesis needs light, but respiration goes on day and night in every living cell.

5. Count the oxygen atoms on the right side of the photosynthesis equation: C6H12O6 + 6O2.

Show answer

Glucose has 6 oxygen atoms. 6O2 has 6 × 2 = 12. Total: 6 + 12 = 18 oxygen atoms (the same as on the left side).
post:
Post Lesson: Cells and Energy

Summary of Key Points

  • Cell theory: all living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; all cells come from existing cells.
  • Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus. Eukaryotes (plants, animals, fungi) have a nucleus and membrane-covered organelles.
  • Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole. Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, and mitochondria.
  • Photosynthesis (chloroplasts): 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
  • Cellular respiration (mitochondria): C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP).
  • The two processes are reverses of each other. Energy flows from sunlight to glucose to ATP to work and heat.

Exit Ticket

1. Which organelle is the site of cellular respiration?

Show answer

The mitochondrion (plural: mitochondria).

2. Name two structures found in plant cells but not in animal cells.

Show answer

Any two: cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole.

3. What are the reactants of photosynthesis?

Show answer

Carbon dioxide and water (with light as the energy source).

4. True or false: plants carry out photosynthesis but not cellular respiration. Explain.

Show answer

False. Plants carry out both. They make glucose by photosynthesis and break it down by cellular respiration in their mitochondria to get ATP.

5. A sealed jar holds a mouse and a green plant in bright light. Explain why the mouse can survive longer than it would in the same jar without the plant.

Show answer

The plant's photosynthesis releases oxygen, which the mouse needs for cellular respiration, and it uses the carbon dioxide that the mouse breathes out.

Reflection

  • Which comparison helps you most remember what organelles do (factory, city, or your own idea)? Write your version for three organelles.
  • Explain to someone at home, in your own words, why the oxygen you breathe and the food you eat both depend on plants.
  • Which was harder for you: the cell parts or the equations? What will you do this week to practice it?

Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. From memory, sketch a plant cell and an animal cell and label at least six parts. Check your sketch against the lesson. (25 min)
Day 2Write both equations from memory three times, then say each one in words. Redo the five Try It problems. (20 min)
Day 3Complete practice items 1–6. For each miss, read the explanation and write one sentence about why the right answer is right. (30 min)
Day 4Complete practice items 7–12. Study the vocabulary list until you can define each term from memory. (30 min)
Day 5Take this week's Practice GED Science test under timed conditions. (90 min, may be split over two days)
Day 6Review every Practice GED question you missed. Sort your mistakes (cell parts, equations, experiments, data) and reread that part of the lesson and Study Notes. (30–40 min)

Test-Taking Strategy: Inputs and Outputs

When a question shows a chemical equation, draw a quick box on your scratch paper with two columns: IN (left of the arrow) and OUT (right of the arrow). Write each substance in the right column before you look at the answer choices. Many wrong answers simply swap a reactant and a product, so this 15-second step protects you from the most common trap.

Study Notes: Cells and Energy

Cell Theory

  1. All living things are made of cells.
  2. The cell is the basic unit of life.
  3. All cells come from existing cells.

Cell Types

Prokaryote (bacteria): no nucleus.
Eukaryote (plants, animals, fungi): nucleus + organelles.

Plant Only

Cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole.

Both Plant and Animal

Membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, ribosomes, ER, Golgi, mitochondria.

Organelle Jobs

  • Nucleus: holds DNA, controls cell
  • Membrane: controls what enters/leaves
  • Ribosome: makes proteins
  • Mitochondrion: respiration, ATP
  • Chloroplast: photosynthesis
  • Vacuole: storage
  • Cell wall: support
PhotosynthesisCellular Respiration
Equation6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP)
WhereChloroplastsMitochondria
WhoPlants, algae, some bacteriaNearly all living things, including plants
WhenOnly in lightAll the time
EnergyStores light energy in glucoseReleases energy from glucose as ATP + heat

Energy flow: sunlight → glucose → ATP → work + heat. Without oxygen: fermentation (2 ATP per glucose; yeast make CO2 + alcohol, muscles make lactic acid).

They placed equal volumes of material in four identical sealed chambers. Each chamber had a sensor that measured carbon dioxide (CO2) in parts per million (ppm). After 20 minutes, they recorded how much the CO2 level had risen in each chamber.

items.prompt: The diagram shows a plant cell with five structures labeled A through E. Which labeled structure is the site of photosynthesis?

figure.alt: Diagram of a boxy plant cell with five labeled parts. A: a round structure containing a smaller dark circle, near the upper left. B: a small oval body with stacked lines inside it, near the lower left (another like it appears at upper right). C: a large shaded sac filling the middle of the cell. D: a small oval body with a folded zigzag inner membrane, near the lower right. E: the thick, stiff outer layer that surrounds the thin inner boundary of the cell.

options: Structure B
Structure A
Structure C
Structure D
items.hint: Photosynthesis happens in the green organelles that contain chlorophyll. Look for the small bodies with stacked lines inside.
items.explain:
Structure B is a chloroplast: a small oval body with stacks of membranes inside (a second one appears at the upper right). Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are where photosynthesis takes place.

  • A is the nucleus (it holds DNA and contains the smaller nucleolus).
  • C is the large central vacuole (storage of water).
  • D is a mitochondrion, recognizable by its folded inner membrane. It carries out cellular respiration, not photosynthesis. This is the most common wrong choice because both organelles deal with energy.
  • E is the cell wall.

items.prompt: Sort each cell structure into the correct category.
items.hint: Three structures help a plant stand up and make its own food. The others are needed by every eukaryotic cell.
items.explain:
• Plant cells only: cell wall (stiff support), chloroplast (photosynthesis), large central vacuole (stores water and keeps the cell firm).
  • Both: nucleus, cell membrane, and mitochondrion.

The most common error is placing the mitochondrion in "plant cells only" or leaving it out of plants. Plants carry out cellular respiration in their mitochondria, just as animals do.

items.prompt: Which statement is one of the main ideas of the cell theory?
options: All cells come from cells that already exist.
All cells contain a nucleus.
All cells contain chloroplasts.
Cells can form from nonliving material such as soil.
items.hint: The cell theory has three parts: what living things are made of, what the basic unit of life is, and where cells come from.
items.explain:
The three parts of the cell theory are: (1) all living things are made of one or more cells; (2) the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; (3) all cells come from existing cells.

"All cells contain a nucleus" is false because bacteria have no nucleus. Only plant and algae cells have chloroplasts, and animal cells do not. The idea that cells form from nonliving material is exactly what the third part of the cell theory rejects.

During photosynthesis, a plant takes in {{0}} from the air and water from the soil. Using energy from sunlight, it makes glucose and releases {{1}}. This process takes place in the {{2}}.

carbon dioxide

items.hint: Write the equation: 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O + light → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub>. Which side shows what goes in?
items.explain:
The equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2.

  • Reactant from the air: carbon dioxide.
  • Product released along with glucose: oxygen.
  • Location: chloroplasts.

The common mistake is reversing the gases (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out), which describes cellular respiration, and placing the process in the mitochondria, which is also where respiration happens.

items.prompt: Heart muscle cells contain far more mitochondria than most other cells in the body. Which statement best explains this?
options: Heart muscle cells work constantly and need a large supply of ATP from cellular respiration.
Heart muscle cells need extra mitochondria to carry out photosynthesis.
Mitochondria store the oxygen that the heart pumps to the rest of the body.
Mitochondria make the proteins that heart muscle cells use to contract.
items.hint: What do mitochondria do, and why would a cell that never stops working need a lot of it?
items.explain:
Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, releasing the energy in glucose as ATP. The heart beats about once every second for a whole lifetime, so its cells need a huge, steady supply of ATP. More mitochondria means more ATP.

Animal cells do not perform photosynthesis. Oxygen is carried by red blood cells, not stored in mitochondria. Proteins are made by ribosomes, so the last choice confuses two organelles.

items.prompt: Which gas is in the bubbles the student counted, and which process produced it?
options: Oxygen, produced by photosynthesis
Carbon dioxide, produced by photosynthesis
Carbon dioxide, produced by cellular respiration
Oxygen, produced by cellular respiration
items.hint: The number of bubbles depended on light. Which process needs light, and what gas does it release?
items.explain:
The bubble count rose with more light and dropped to 0 in the dark. Photosynthesis needs light and releases oxygen (6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2).

Cellular respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, and it does not depend on light, so it cannot explain bubbles that disappear in the dark. Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide; it does not produce it.

items.prompt: What is the mean number of bubbles per minute when the lamp was 30 cm from the plant? Enter a number.
items.hint: Add the three trials at 30 cm, then divide by the number of trials.
items.explain:
Trials at 30 cm: 14, 12, and 16 bubbles per minute.

14 + 12 + 16 = 42

42 ÷ 3 = 14 bubbles per minute

Check: 14 is between the 20 cm mean (23) and the 40 cm mean (8), which fits the trend. A common error is forgetting to divide (42) or dividing by 5 because the table has five rows.

items.prompt: Why did the student keep the plant at 22 °C during every trial?
options: So that any change in bubble count could be linked to the amount of light rather than to a change in temperature
So that temperature would be the dependent variable in the experiment
So that the plant would carry out cellular respiration instead of photosynthesis
So that the plant would produce the same number of bubbles at every distance
items.hint: A lamp gives off heat as well as light. What could happen to the water if the lamp were moved very close?
items.explain:
The independent variable is the amount of light (lamp distance). A lamp close to the plant would also warm the water, and temperature can affect the rate of photosynthesis. Holding the temperature at 22 °C makes it a controlled variable, so it cannot act as a confounding variable.

The dependent variable is the number of bubbles, not temperature. Keeping temperature constant does not switch the plant from one process to another. And the goal was not identical bubble counts; the student expected the counts to change with light.

items.prompt: Which two conclusions are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: The rate of oxygen production decreased as the lamp was moved farther from the plant.
Light is needed for the plant to produce oxygen bubbles.
Moving the lamp from 10 cm to 20 cm cut the rate of oxygen production in half.
Light is the only factor that affects the rate of photosynthesis.
The plant stopped all cellular activity when the lamp was off.
The plant would produce more bubbles at 50 cm than at 40 cm.
items.hint: Check each statement against the numbers. Reject any statement about something the student did not test.
items.explain:
Supported:

  • The means fall as distance increases: 33, 23, 14, 8 bubbles per minute.
  • With the lamp off, there were 0 bubbles in all three trials, while every lit trial produced bubbles.

Not supported:

  • Half of 33 is 16.5, but the 20 cm mean is 23, so the rate did not drop by half.
  • Only light was tested; temperature and carbon dioxide were held constant, so the data cannot show that light is the only factor.
  • Zero bubbles means no oxygen was released. The plant's cells were still alive and carrying out cellular respiration in the dark.
  • The trend predicts fewer bubbles at 50 cm, not more.

items.prompt: What was the purpose of Chamber 4, which held glass beads?
options: To show that any rise in carbon dioxide in the other chambers came from the living peas and not from the chamber or sensor
To provide the peas in the other chambers with extra oxygen for cellular respiration
To test whether glass beads carry out cellular respiration faster at 20 °C than at 10 °C
To serve as a second independent variable along with temperature
items.hint: Glass beads are not alive. What would a change in CO<sub>2</sub> in that chamber tell you about the equipment?
items.explain:
Chamber 4 is the control. Glass beads take up the same volume as the peas but are not alive, so they cannot respire. Its CO2 rose by 0 ppm, which shows that the sealed chamber and sensor did not produce or leak in CO2 on their own. So the rises in Chambers 1–3 can be credited to the peas.

The beads are in a separate sealed chamber, so they cannot supply oxygen to the peas. Beads are nonliving, so they do not respire at any temperature, and they were only tested at 20 °C. A control group is a baseline for comparison, not an extra independent variable.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Germinating peas carry out cellular respiration faster than dry peas, and cooling germinating peas from 20 °C to 10 °C slows their respiration.
Dry peas are not alive, because they did not release any carbon dioxide.
Germinating peas release carbon dioxide only when the temperature is 20 °C.
Germinating peas released carbon dioxide because they were carrying out photosynthesis.
items.hint: Compare Chamber 1 with Chamber 3, then Chamber 1 with Chamber 2. Then check each choice against the exact numbers.
items.explain:
Cellular respiration releases CO2, so a bigger CO2 rise means faster respiration.

  • At 20 °C: germinating peas 1,200 ppm vs. dry peas 100 ppm. 1,200 ÷ 100 = 12, so germinating peas respired about 12 times as fast. Growing seeds need much more energy (ATP).
  • Germinating peas: 1,200 ppm at 20 °C vs. 540 ppm at 10 °C, so cooling slowed respiration.

Dry peas did release CO2 (100 ppm vs. 0 for the beads), so they were alive and respiring slowly. Germinating peas released 540 ppm at 10 °C, so they do not release CO2 only at 20 °C. Photosynthesis uses CO2; it does not release it.

items.prompt: A student wrote this summary of the pea experiment. Click the sentence that makes a claim the data do NOT support.
spans: We measured how much carbon dioxide built up in four sealed chambers over 20 minutes.
The glass beads caused no change in carbon dioxide, so the equipment did not add any carbon dioxide on its own.
At 20 °C, germinating peas released 12 times as much carbon dioxide as dry peas.
Germinating peas released less carbon dioxide at 10 °C than at 20 °C.
This proves that warmer temperatures always speed up cellular respiration in every kind of living thing.
The dry peas released a small amount of carbon dioxide, which suggests they were respiring slowly.
items.hint: Look for a sentence that goes beyond what was tested. How many kinds of organisms and how many temperatures were in this experiment?
items.explain:
The experiment tested only one kind of organism (peas) at only two temperatures (10 °C and 20 °C). It cannot show what happens in "every kind of living thing" or at all temperatures. In fact, very high temperatures damage cells and slow respiration. Words like "proves," "always," and "every" are warning signs of an overgeneralization.

The other sentences match the data: the beads showed 0 ppm; 1,200 ÷ 100 = 12; 540 ppm is less than 1,200 ppm; and dry peas released 100 ppm.
